editions.title: Chip crunch deepens as Altman meets Samsung; Binance outflows
editions.notification: Memory chip shortage deepens as Sam Altman meets Samsung, and Binance users pull $3.6bn after its heist.
editions.intro:
The memory chip shortage dominated the last 24 hours. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman met roughly 50 Samsung executives at the company's Yongin site on Saturday, with Samsung confirming the talks covered how AI could reshape industries and business. No supply deals were announced, though memory supply is widely assumed to have been on the agenda. The meeting fits a wider pattern: Samsung and SK hynix are signing long-term customer agreements years ahead, with SK hynix saying its DRAM and HBM output is effectively sold out through 2029, yet both shares remain well below their 52-week highs.

Crypto was the other major theme. Binance users withdrew about $3.6bn as the exchange restarted services after a heist. The FBI and TRM Labs attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, and Binance says it has found further breach points. Binance has pledged to reimburse users whose assets were stolen. Separately, French lawmakers voted narrowly to add a traffic-based levy on content providers to the 2027 budget. The amendment still has to clear further budget stages, and the government opposed it.

Elsewhere, Intel and AMD may be exploring cooperation, though neither has confirmed details. Spotify is reportedly preparing an AI product with a possible premium surcharge, and Apple's first results under CEO John Ternus are due on 2 November. Most other items are rumours or product news with limited near-term market impact.

top_stories.summary: A narrow 11-10 committee vote added a levy of about $0.06 per gigabyte on content providers to France's 2027 budget. The measure would cover content delivery networks and still faces further budget votes, with the government opposed.

editions.title: Amazon's AI spend, Microsoft buyouts and a neocloud wobble
editions.notification: Amazon's AWS grew 39% but free cash flow turned deeply negative. Here is why AI spending is squeezing Big Tech.
editions.intro:
Amazon dominated the period. Its third-quarter results showed Amazon Web Services growing 39% to $46bn, with a backlog of $578bn, but revenue and earnings per share came in slightly below forecasts and shares fell as much as 7% in extended trading. Free cash flow over the past year slipped to minus $42.4bn, largely from AI capital spending. Chief executive Andy Jassy said AWS should grow more than 40% in 2027 and 2028 and that Amazon will spend meaningfully more on AI next year.

The cash squeeze is a wider theme. A Reuters analysis of LSEG data finds that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned the smallest share of their cash to shareholders in at least 15 years, with buybacks down 83%. Their combined capital spending of $556.9bn exceeded operating cash flow, leaving a free cash flow deficit of $14bn. Meanwhile Microsoft is offering voluntary severance to about 60,000 staff while protecting AI-critical teams, and its AI infrastructure budget is about $170bn for 2026.

Doubts about the AI build-out are growing. Shares in neocloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have fallen by about a quarter in a month, and Nvidia quietly lowered published bandwidth targets for its Vera Rubin hardware. Reports also say OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10bn. Against that backdrop, Oracle shares rose about 14% during its AI World conference, though they remain well below their late 2025 high.

top_stories.title: AWS grows 39% but Amazon's cash burn deepens
top_stories.summary: Amazon posted record operating margins and a 39% jump in AWS revenue, but results were slightly below forecasts and shares fell sharply after hours. Free cash flow of minus $42.4bn shows how heavily AI spending is weighing on the business, and Jassy signalled more investment in 2027.

editions.title: DoorDash buys Instacart; tech sell-off deepens over AI spending
editions.notification: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for about $17bn as AI spending worries rattle tech stocks.
editions.intro:
The biggest development is DoorDash's agreed deal to buy rival Instacart at $65 a share, a 26% premium, valuing the business at roughly $17 billion. The cash-heavy offer still needs regulatory and shareholder approval, and it would leave iPhone users with one fewer app-based grocery and delivery option. The deal lands amid a sharp slide in US tech shares, with the Nasdaq posting its worst month since March 2025.

That selloff is driven by fears about the roughly $800 billion that Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon and Microsoft are committing to spending in 2026. Intel fell 28% after warning of weaker PC demand, while Reddit dropped 29% after weak user numbers and complaints that Google's AI search is cutting its referral traffic. Reddit's CEO said Google's AI Mode does not drive meaningful traffic, and Alphabet's core ad growth slowed to its weakest pace in five quarters even as it kept capex guidance of up to $205 billion.

The AI nervousness also shows up in private markets. The Financial Times reports that OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10 billion, citing the AI selloff and Anthropic's forthcoming listing; Anthropic's IPO filing, meanwhile, shows $16.3 billion of first-half revenue alongside heavy losses. Apple, by contrast, retook the title of the world's most valuable listed company, supported by iPhone demand and its China AI rollout.

editions.title: Alphabet sheds $500bn as AI spending doubts hit Big Tech and Intel crashes
editions.notification: Alphabet loses $500bn in a day as AI spending doubts spread; Intel slumps on weak PC outlook.
editions.intro:
Investor patience with AI spending cracked this week. Alphabet lost just over $500bn in value after its quarterly update showed AI summaries in search weighing on advertising, with free cash flow negative by over $9bn. Amazon's free cash flow also swung deeply negative and its shares fell in after-hours trading, while Microsoft's shares barely moved despite 19% revenue growth. A global tech sell-off was reported to be deepening as the Nikkei and Wall Street opened lower.

Intel was the sharpest casualty. Its shares fell by roughly a quarter after third-quarter client chip revenue dropped and the company guided fourth-quarter revenue and earnings below expectations, blaming a memory shortage that is squeezing PC demand. Intel expects the PC market to shrink 12% this year. Reddit, meanwhile, said search referrals had fallen sharply and it will move to a logged-in-only experience, a direct example of how AI search is reshaping traffic.

Crypto was hit by a major security failure. Binance said an attacker drained hot wallets, with the affected amount put at about $6.3bn, and it pledged to cover losses from its SAFU fund and company money. Separately, reports that Nvidia's chief executive had ties to a Singapore businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of helping Beijing are unverified and have been strongly denied by Nvidia. Dealmaking continued, with DoorDash agreeing to buy Instacart for about $17bn and the FCC approving Amazon's Globalstar acquisition.

top_stories.summary: Alphabet fell almost 13% to a six-month low after AI summaries in search were blamed for weaker ad revenue, even though Google Cloud grew 103%. Amazon also fell after-hours on negative free cash flow, while Microsoft held up better. The reaction shows investors increasingly questioning the payoff from heavy AI spending.

top_stories.summary: Intel shares fell almost a quarter after client revenue fell and fourth-quarter guidance missed estimates by a wide margin. Chief executive Lip-Bu Tan blamed memory shortages and supply constraints, and forecast the PC market shrinking 12% this year. The stock had more than doubled earlier this year, so the drop is steep.

top_stories.summary: Attackers drained Binance hot wallets, with the affected funds put at around $6.3bn, and Tether and Circle froze stablecoins to help. Binance says the likely entry point was a compromised engineer's laptop and has pledged to cover all customer losses. The SAFU reserve covers only a fraction of the amount, so company funds will carry much of the cost.

editions.title: Alphabet's $500bn slide and Intel's crash rattle tech
editions.notification: Alphabet loses $500bn as AI spending doubts spread; Intel and Binance also reel
editions.intro:
Wall Street's tech earnings season turned sharply on Thursday as investors questioned how much AI spending will pay off. Alphabet shed just over $500bn in value, falling almost 13% to a six-month low, after its quarterly update showed AI summaries in search weighing on advertising revenue. Profits fell 25% and free cash flow was negative by more than $9bn, even though Google Cloud grew 103%. Amazon and Microsoft also reported strong top lines, but Amazon's free cash flow was deeply negative and its shares fell about 6% after hours, and a global tech sell-off was reported to be deepening.

Intel was the other major casualty. Its shares fell by almost a quarter after a steep drop in PC chip sales and a weak fourth-quarter forecast, with the chief executive blaming a memory-chip shortage and warning the PC market could shrink 12% this year. Datacentre and AI revenue rose 78%, but the company said it will likely not fully meet datacentre demand in the first half. Memory costs are a common thread, also hitting PC makers and smartphone shipments, which fell 20% in the third quarter.

Crypto and security stories dominated the rest of the day. Binance said an attacker drained hot wallets, with the affected funds now put at about $6.3bn; Tether and Circle froze stablecoin balances, and Binance has pledged to cover losses. Separately, a New York Times report alleging that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had ties to a Singapore businesswoman suspected of helping Beijing was met with Nvidia's denial. Several linked Nvidia items, including reported credit guarantees for Nscale, remain unconfirmed rumours.

editions.title: Binance hack, Alphabet rout and Intel slump rattle tech
editions.notification: Binance hit by a roughly $6.3bn crypto theft as Alphabet and Intel shares tumble on AI doubts.
editions.intro:
Markets and security were the dominant stories over the last 24 hours. Binance said an attacker drained its hot wallets, with the affected funds later put at about $6.3 billion. Tether and Circle froze significant stablecoin balances to help, and Binance has pledged to cover all losses from its SAFU fund and company money. The exchange blamed a likely entry point via a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, and withdrawals remain paused while it overhauls security. A crypto industry figure has said the bitcoin is probably unrecoverable, though that is an opinion rather than an official update.

Earnings reshaped the market mood. Alphabet lost just over $500bn in value after AI summaries in search weighed on ad revenue, even as Google Cloud grew 103%. Amazon's free cash flow turned sharply negative and its shares fell in after-hours trading. Intel dropped almost a quarter of its value after PC chip sales fell, with its CEO warning the PC chip market could shrink 12% next year. Taken together, investors are increasingly questioning how much AI spending will pay back.

Nvidia was the subject of several reports. The Information says it is in talks to guarantee billions of dollars of debt for Nscale's West Virginia data centre, which Anthropic plans to use under a deal worth about $45 billion. Separately, a New York Times report alleges US intelligence suspected a Singapore executive of acting for Beijing and linked her to Jensen Huang; Nvidia and the Chinese embassy have denied wrongdoing, and the claims rest on unnamed sources.

top_stories.summary: Binance said an attacker drained hot wallets and later put the affected funds at about $6.3bn. Tether and Circle froze large stablecoin balances, and Binance has pledged to cover all losses while withdrawals stay paused for a security overhaul. The SAFU fund covers only about a sixth of the amount.

top_stories.title: Alphabet loses $500bn as AI search fears hit ads
top_stories.summary: Alphabet shares fell almost 13% to a six-month low after AI summaries weighed on search ad revenue and profits fell 25%. Google Cloud grew 103%, but free cash flow was negative. Amazon also fell after its results showed a $42bn negative free cash flow.

top_stories.title: Intel shares sink a quarter on PC chip slump
top_stories.summary: Intel fell almost a quarter after client computing revenue dropped and the CEO warned PC chip demand could shrink 12% next year. Datacenter and AI sales grew 78%, but supply constraints mean it may not fully meet datacenter demand in the first half.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly weighs credit backing for Nscale deal
top_stories.summary: The Information reports Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions of dollars of debt for Nscale's 460MW West Virginia campus tied to Anthropic's $45bn compute deal. Nothing is signed, and the report comes as scrutiny of AI data centre financing grows.

top_stories.title: NYT links Jensen Huang to Megaspeed executive under suspicion
top_stories.summary: The New York Times reports Nvidia's chief executive had close ties with a Megaspeed director whom US intelligence suspects of acting for Beijing. There is no evidence Huang knew of the suspicions, Nvidia says the contacts were ordinary business, and the claims rest on unnamed sources.

top_stories.title: Data on 41,000 DHS staff leaked online
top_stories.summary: Personal details of more than 41,000 Department of Homeland Security staff, including immigration agents, were published after a group claimed access via Okta single sign-on. DHS says it is investigating, while Okta says it sees no evidence its systems were compromised.

top_stories.title: Reddit moves towards logged-in-only experience
top_stories.summary: Reddit's CEO said the platform is moving to a logged-in-only experience, with tests in select non-US markets from Q4. Falling search referrals prompted the change, and the company warned daily active uniques could drop by a low double-digit percentage in Q4 if trends continue.

rumour_watch.note: A brief XenoSpectrum report says the US Department of Justice is questioning industry players on Nvidia's $12.9bn Hugging Face deal; antitrust questioning is early-stage and no formal case is confirmed.
Only a headline from a Korean outlet is available, duplicating the NYT allegations with no new evidence, so it adds little credibility.
A brief Digitimes report on 10-year DRAM deals by Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance is plausible given the memory shortage but lacks detail.
An anonymous Foxconn claim about relaxed iPhone Duo quality checks is weakly sourced, relies on a translated secondary report, and Apple has not responded.

in_brief.line: The FCC approved Amazon's $11.5bn Globalstar acquisition, giving it spectrum for a planned direct-to-device satellite system.
Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 more countries and launching multiturn ads in the US as search shifts to AI answers.
T-Mobile's CEO said there is no room for an MVNO deal with SpaceX, though a commercial or resale arrangement remains open.
Intel says its budget Wildcat Lake laptop chips are sold out, and it expects no memory supply improvement in 2027.
The FTC and eight states sued Toast over hidden fees and hard-to-cancel subscriptions; Toast disputes the claims.
Reuters reports Amazon cut a small number of devices and services roles, reportedly no more than 250 people.
Kaspersky says Lazarus malware now uses post-quantum ML-KEM-1024 key exchange in a campaign targeting South Korean organisations.
The Pentagon released a full-resolution image of a Chinese spaceplane resembling the X-37B, taken by a commercial satellite in 2024.

Finance.title: Tech sell-off rattles markets as AI spending fears mount
Finance.notification: Tech stocks slump as AI spending fears spread from Wall Street to Europe and London
Finance.summary:
A heavy tech sell-off has dominated markets. The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5 per cent in one session, with Intel down about 30 per cent after a weak revenue forecast, and investors increasingly question the cash burn behind AI projects. Europe's tech index fell 2.75 per cent, while the STOXX 600 slipped 0.36 per cent despite its best month since June.

Wider unease is visible across the Atlantic and in Asia. Nasdaq ended October with its worst month in over a year, and the OpenAI fundraising target has been cut by $10 billion. Markets then steadied somewhat as a rebound took hold, though analysts expect further volatility. Oil has eased on hopes of renewed US-Iran talks, with Brent falling to about $111 a barrel, which lifted Indian shares.

Crypto has been hit hardest by the Binance hack, with about $6.3 billion stolen. Binance says it has replenished around 90 per cent of the losses, but outflows and a weaker bitcoin price show the strain. In the UK, the Poundland collapse and possible Bank of England easing of mortgage limits are the main domestic stories.

highlights.text: The Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5% in a session driven by AI cash-burn fears, and the index had its worst month in over a year.

highlights.text: Poundland is heading towards administration, with up to 12,000 direct jobs at risk and a break-up seen as most likely.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: The Bank of England is reportedly exploring easing its limit on higher-risk mortgage lending, though no decision has been announced.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Fitch kept France at A+ but moved the outlook to negative, citing weaker growth, a wider deficit and political fragmentation.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Sensex and Nifty rallied as Brent crude fell towards $111 on Iran-US talks, and Reliance posted a 40.6% jump in quarterly profit.

TRM Labs and Chainalysis say North Korea's Lazarus Group is the likely culprit behind the Binance theft.
The Nasdaq 100 closed October with its worst performance since 2025 after disappointing tech earnings.
Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent in several cities, with shops looted in Frankfurt and police clashes.
Deutsche Bank plans to close 20% of its German branches as it shifts towards digital banking.
Chinese shares rebounded from their worst sell-off in about a decade on hopes of state support, though details are unconfirmed.

World.title: US midterms enter final days as Iran tensions and oil risks build
World.notification: Trump's final midterm push, a Michigan Senate feud and Iran threats are converging ahead of Tuesday's vote
World.summary:
The US midterm elections on Tuesday dominate the day's political news. Donald Trump has held a final round of rallies and tele-rallies, focusing on attacks on Democrats while living costs, particularly fuel, groceries and health care, weigh on voters. A Harvard forecasting tool gives Democrats a 96% chance of taking the House and 76% of the Senate. In Michigan, Representative Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after losing the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, a move that has angered party leaders and could shape a race seen as crucial for Senate control.

Alongside the campaign, the Iran confrontation is raising risks for energy markets. Iran's supreme leader has warned the US and Israel against new strikes, promising a response without geographical limits, while reports of mines hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have pushed crude prices higher. Diplomacy through mediators continues, but neither side has shifted its position.

Markets are watching two threads at once: a possible shift in Congress that could constrain Trump's agenda, and a renewed Gulf conflict that could keep oil and defence stocks firm while weighing on equities. Elsewhere, Europe faces protests over living costs in France and Germany, and Poland's court dispute is escalating.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Trump's final rallies centre on attacking Democrats, while Harvard's tool gives Democrats a strong chance of taking the House and a narrower lead in the Senate.

highlights.text: Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent with shop looting in Frankfurt, following youth-led unrest in France ahead of 31 October.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: US, South Korea and Japan reaffirmed demands for complete North Korean denuclearisation, as speculation grows about a Trump-Kim meeting at APEC.

Rachel Reeves argues Britain's future lies in the EU, while Labour's manifesto rules out rejoining.
Police arrest at least 139 at a London protest against the Palestine Action ban before a Supreme Court appeal.

Tech.title: AI spending squeezes Big Tech cash and buybacks
Tech.notification: Big Tech buybacks fell 83% as AI spending eats the cash. Here is what it means for investors.
Tech.summary:
The defining theme in tech right now is the cost of the AI build-out. A Reuters analysis of LSEG data shows Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned the smallest share of their cash to shareholders in at least 15 years, with buybacks down 83%. Their combined capital spending doubled to $556.9bn, more than their operating cash flow, leaving a free cash flow deficit of $14bn. Amazon's results point the same way: AWS grew 39%, but free cash flow over the past year turned negative and shares fell in extended trading.

Doubts about returns are growing. Investors are reportedly trimming growth exposure, neocloud shares such as CoreWeave have fallen by about a quarter in a month, and Howard Marks says recent AI setbacks have dented the sector's aura. OpenAI has reportedly cut its fundraising target by $10bn, while Nvidia quietly lowered published bandwidth figures for its Vera Rubin hardware.

Memory chips are the strongest counterpoint. Samsung and SK hynix posted record combined third-quarter operating profit and are locking in long-term customer deals, though both shares remain well below their 52-week highs and analysts warn of a possible glut around 2028.

highlights.text: AWS grew 39% to $46bn, but shares fell as much as 7% after hours as free cash flow turned negative on AI spending.

Fashion.title: Europe's luxury houses hit hard by China slump
Fashion.notification: Europe's luxury giants have lost over €250bn in value this year as China demand falters.
Fashion.summary:
Europe's luxury houses are under pressure from China, where a slowing economy, a property-led fall in household wealth and a shift away from logo-led buying have hit sales. A Telegraph feature says LVMH, Hermès, Kering, Richemont, Prada and Moncler have together lost over €250bn in market value this year, with LVMH's fashion division down in the mid-teens in China in the third quarter and Kering's China sales down 15 to 20%.

Brands are looking for growth elsewhere. North America is a bright spot: Zegna Americas rose 14%, Hermès Americas 8.8% in the third quarter and Kering's North American sales 1%. Analysts expect the US midterm elections to have only a minor effect on spending, though consumer confidence is weak. Investment in the US continues while Europe faces unrest and the Middle East remains soft.

Elsewhere, the sector is looking for new routes to growth. Turkey's Desa has launched Nuera to commercialise Gozen's biofabricated leather Lunaform, with first orders from Kering, and Palace and Burberry are releasing a limited capsule. Lacoste, Kiton and Louis Vuitton have also made retail and product moves.

highlights.label: China
highlights.text: Mid-teens fall at LVMH fashion and 15-20% drop at Kering in China as slowdown, property losses and a shift from logos bite.
